messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 73
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Photos): Related photos, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself, Freeze When Threatened: freeze completely when feeling threatened
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Raymond, a seventy-three-year-old journalist who had spent decades covering city hall and local politics, had been in the room when the ceiling collapsed. It had been a routine press conference in a municipal building that everyone assumed was safe, and then the roar came, and the dust, and the screaming, and the weight of concrete and rebar driving him to the floor with a force that stole his breath and his sense of where he was. He had crawled out over broken bodies, his hands slick with blood that was not his own, and for months afterward he told himself he was fine. He was a journalist. He had seen things. He knew how to compartmentalize.

But the memory did not stay in its compartment. It came back as a film that played over and over, always the same sequence—the vibration in his feet, the split second of silence before the roar, the taste of plaster dust and copper that coated his tongue and that he could still summon without warning. When he smelled damp concrete or caught a whiff of something metallic, his mouth would fill with that taste and he would be back in the room, the weight pressing down, the darkness so complete he could not tell if his eyes were open or closed. The story felt unreal even as it replayed. It was so extreme, so far outside anything he had ever expected to survive, that part of him still did not believe it had happened to him at all. And yet when the memory seized him, he was not remembering it—he was living it, his heart hammering, his hands trembling, his throat tight with the certainty that something terrible was about to happen again.

Raymond had come to believe that if he let himself think about the event deliberately, he would not be able to handle it. The thoughts were like a door he dared not open, because once opened, he was sure they would pour out and never stop. He had also become certain that he would never feel normal emotions again. The world had gone flat. Nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore—not his work, which he had stopped taking seriously, not his relationships, which had dwindled to occasional phone calls with his ex-wife, not the books he used to read or the jazz he used to love. He felt hollowed out, a shell of the man he had been.

He began to change how he lived. At home, he listened constantly for sounds that might mean someone was entering—a creak in the hallway, a click at the lock, the whisper of a footstep on the carpet. He could not relax even when he knew he was safe. He sat with his back against the wall in every room, positioning himself so he could see the door, the windows, the whole space. In restaurants, he scanned for exits and noted the placement of knives on nearby tables, the weight of a salt shaker, the heft of a glass. He noticed potential weapons everywhere, not because he planned to use them but because his eyes went to them automatically, cataloguing what could hurt him and what could not.

He started spending money impulsively. It began as a way to distract himself—a new television, a watch he did not need, a subscription to a streaming service he never watched. The purchases gave him a few minutes of relief, a small spike of something that felt almost like pleasure, but the feeling faded quickly and left him with bills he could not afford and a growing sense of shame. He told himself he would stop, but when the urge came—usually after a memory had ambushed him, or when he found himself frozen in a grocery aisle because an unpredictable sound had triggered the film again—he could not resist.

The freezing was the worst. When something caught him off guard—a car backfiring, a door slamming, a voice too loud—his body would lock. He could not move, could not speak, could not even turn his head. He would stand or sit perfectly still, his breath shallow, his eyes wide, waiting for whatever was coming. It might last thirty seconds or three minutes, and afterward he would feel exhausted and foolish, but he could not stop it from happening.

His work suffered. He stopped taking assignments that required him to go to unfamiliar buildings or cover events with large crowds. He turned down a story about infrastructure safety because the thought of walking into another municipal building made his stomach clench. His editor noticed. Raymond was put on a reduced schedule, then asked to take leave. He told himself he did not care, but the loss of his routine only made the days longer and emptier.

What finally brought him to seek help was a morning in his apartment when the film played three times before noon. He had been sitting with his back to the wall, listening to the silence, and he had thought: I cannot keep living like this. He was afraid of what therapy might stir up—afraid that talking about the event would open that door he had kept so carefully shut—but he was also afraid of what would happen if he did not. He wanted to believe that somewhere underneath the flatness and the fear, the man he used to be was still there. He wanted to find a way back to meaning. He was not sure it was possible, but he had come anyway, and that, for now, was enough.
